title: Intelligent Knowledge Graph Visualization
problem: Knowledge graphs reveal relationships, dependencies and hidden patterns in enterprise applications, but exploring them often requires Cypher queries and knowledge of Neo4j. Build an intuitive, interactive, AI-assisted knowledge graph visualization platform that lets technical and non-technical users explore those relationships without knowing graph databases or query languages. The interface should make complex knowledge understandable instead of overwhelming users with thousands of nodes.
audience: Developers, architects and business users who need to understand enterprise application relationships and the effects of changes.
outcome: Make complex enterprise application knowledge accessible through clear visual exploration, natural-language questions, contextual insights and component-level impact analysis.

required.title: Clear, interactive graph views
required.text: Present complex knowledge graphs through clean, easy-to-understand visualizations. Avoid exposing thousands of nodes at once without a useful way to understand them.

required.title: Natural-language exploration
required.text: Let users ask questions such as: which programs depend on a COBOL module; which business rules relate to a database table; and which components would be affected by modifying a field.

required.title: Multiple abstraction levels
required.text: Support navigation from high-level application architecture down to individual programs, functions, variables and their dependencies.

required.title: Smart graph navigation
required.text: Provide search, filtering, grouping, zooming and progressive expansion of relationships so users can investigate the relevant part of a graph.

required.title: AI-powered insights
required.text: Use AI to summarize relationships, explain dependencies and highlight the potential impacts of a change.

required.title: Visual impact analysis
required.text: Let a user select a component and instantly visualize its upstream and downstream dependencies.

required.title: Live Neo4j integration
required.text: Connect to an existing Neo4j knowledge graph and dynamically retrieve the relevant nodes and relationships.

workflow: Connect to a Neo4j graph → search or ask a natural-language question → inspect a simplified application-level view → filter, group, zoom and expand relationships → drill into programs, functions or variables → select a component to inspect upstream/downstream impact and AI explanations.

deliverables.title: Working visualization prototype
deliverables.text: Demonstrate a modern, intuitive knowledge graph interface that makes complex enterprise application knowledge accessible to technical and non-technical users, including graph navigation, Neo4j integration and AI-assisted exploration.

success.title: User experience — 25%
success.text: Simplicity, clarity and ease of navigation.

success.title: Visualization innovation — 25%
success.text: Creative approaches to representing complex relationships.

success.title: Technical implementation — 20%
success.text: Neo4j integration, performance and scalability.

success.title: AI capabilities — 15%
success.text: Natural-language querying and contextual insights.

success.title: Practical usability — 15%
success.text: Effectiveness in understanding real-world application dependencies.

scope.title: Enterprise application knowledge
scope.text: The graph may represent COBOL programs, database schemas, business rules and application dependencies. Participants may use sample datasets representing these elements.

scope.title: Accessible exploration
scope.text: The platform must let users explore the graph without requiring graph-database or query-language knowledge; the solution should simplify complex views while retaining meaningful relationships.

title: Next-Generation Interactive Code Visualization Platform
problem: Static diagrams can show workflows and architecture, but large enterprise codebases need richer exploration. Build an intelligent, interactive code visualization platform that automatically turns source code into navigable representations of application architecture, dependencies, business logic and execution workflows. Understanding a codebase should feel as intuitive as exploring an interactive map, without manually defining all its diagrams.
audience: People exploring an existing enterprise codebase and reviewing its architecture, dependencies, business logic or change impacts.
outcome: Move from source code to accurate, interactive views that support drill-down, workflow exploration, bidirectional source navigation and AI-assisted understanding.

required.title: Automatic visualization from source
required.text: Analyze source code and automatically generate architecture diagrams, dependency maps, call graphs and execution workflows rather than requiring manually defined diagrams.

required.title: Interactive drill-down
required.text: Let users zoom, navigate, filter and progressively drill down from application-level architecture to individual modules, functions and statements.

required.title: Code dependency mapping
required.text: Visualize relationships between programs, modules, functions, databases, APIs and external systems, including upstream and downstream dependencies.

required.title: Dynamic workflow visualization
required.text: Generate interactive control-flow and business-process diagrams covering execution paths, conditional branches, data transformations and interactions between components.

required.title: Natural-language code understanding
required.text: Support questions about a complete customer-transaction workflow, modules affected by a function change, data flowing from an API to a database, and dependencies of a COBOL program.

required.title: Bidirectional code navigation
required.text: Clicking a diagram component should open its corresponding source code. Selecting source code should highlight its position in the visualization.

required.title: Intelligent simplification
required.text: Automatically group related components, hide unnecessary detail and provide different abstraction levels so complex diagrams do not overwhelm users.

required.title: Language extensibility
required.text: Design support for modern and legacy programming languages, including Java, Python, COBOL and FORTRAN. The demonstration may use one programming language, provided the architecture is designed for extensibility.

required.title: Export for documentation and reviews
required.text: Enable visualization exports to formats such as SVG, PNG or interactive HTML for documentation and architecture reviews.

workflow: Load an existing codebase → generate architecture, dependency and workflow views → navigate and simplify the map → drill into modules, functions or statements → move between diagrams and matching source code → ask an AI-assisted question or inspect a change impact → export a visualization for review.

deliverables.title: Working visualization prototype
deliverables.text: Automatically generate interactive visualizations from an existing codebase, showing application architecture and component relationships, code dependencies and call graphs, and business logic and execution workflows.

deliverables.title: Interactive source and AI demonstration
deliverables.text: Demonstrate navigation between diagrams and source code, AI-assisted exploration and impact analysis. One programming language is sufficient for the demo when the architecture supports extension to others.

success.title: Visualization innovation and user experience — 30%
success.text: The quality and innovation of the visual exploration experience.

success.title: Code and dependency accuracy — 25%
success.text: Accuracy of the code analysis and dependency relationships represented.

success.title: Interactive navigation and workflow exploration — 20%
success.text: Effective navigation through source-linked diagrams and execution workflows.

success.title: AI-assisted understanding and insights — 15%
success.text: The usefulness of AI-assisted exploration, explanations and change-impact insights.

success.title: Scalability and extensibility — 10%
success.text: Ability to extend the approach to larger codebases and additional languages.

scope.title: Beyond static diagrams
scope.text: The platform should analyze source code and produce rich, navigable application views, rather than functioning only as a manually authored static-diagram tool.

scope.title: A bounded language demonstration
scope.text: Participants may demonstrate one programming language while designing an extensible architecture for modern and legacy languages.

title: Quantum-Readiness Network Map
problem: Supply-chain signatures, certificates and secure connections rely on public-key cryptography such as RSA and elliptic curves. Some signed records must remain trustworthy for 10–30 years, while a company's suppliers, carriers and customs partners may migrate to post-quantum cryptography at different speeds. Existing inventory tools mostly inspect one organization's own cryptography. Build a tool that assesses, ranks and visualizes quantum-readiness across a supplier network using limited and incomplete information, including partners unwilling to share internal details.
audience: Procurement, supply-chain risk and security teams assessing cryptographic dependencies across suppliers and other partners.
outcome: Help a non-expert identify partners relying on quantum-vulnerable cryptography, prioritize upgrades by business risk and understand downstream effects or dependencies when a partner changes.

required.title: Assess partner readiness
required.text: Assess each partner's quantum-readiness using the data actually available. The tool must work with limited and incomplete partner information.

required.title: Rank partners by risk
required.text: Consider how long a partner's records must remain trustworthy, what flows through that partner, and the difficulty of migration when ranking risks and upgrade priorities.

required.title: Confidence for every assessment
required.text: Show confidence for every assessment. When evidence is thin, say so rather than silently guessing.

required.title: A non-expert network view
required.text: Visualize where the largest risks sit across the network, including how one lagging supplier affects partners downstream of it.

required.title: Useful prioritization answers
required.text: Help users understand which partners still depend on cryptography expected to be vulnerable to quantum computing, which matter most because of record lifetimes, where upgrades should be requested first and who might be affected when an upgrade occurs.

workflow: Collect available supplier-network and cryptographic information → assess each partner's readiness → attach confidence and expose missing evidence → rank risks using record lifetime, flows and migration difficulty → visualize downstream dependencies → identify upgrade priorities and affected partners.

deliverables.title: Working readiness-assessment prototype
deliverables.text: Provide a web UI, CLI or API prototype that assesses each partner, ranks risk, shows confidence for every assessment and visualizes the network for non-expert users.

success.title: Risk-ranking accuracy
success.text: Accuracy of the partner risk ranking.

success.title: Handling uncertainty
success.text: Clear, defensible treatment of incomplete evidence and assessment confidence.

success.title: Prioritization logic
success.text: Useful reasoning about which partners should upgrade first.

success.title: Usability and presentation clarity
success.text: A network view and explanation that a non-expert can understand.

constraints.title: Incomplete information is part of the challenge
constraints.text: Do not assume every partner will disclose internal cryptographic details. The assessment must make limited evidence and uncertainty visible.

scope.title: Supply-chain cryptographic dependencies
scope.text: Relevant examples include signed bills of lading, certificates of origin, quality records, device identities and partner APIs. Long-lived aerospace, pharmaceutical or defence records illustrate why record trust periods matter.

scope.title: A network, not one isolated organization
scope.text: Assess readiness across a partner network, recognizing that a manufacturer can depend on hundreds of suppliers, carriers and customs systems and that a slow critical partner can affect the wider chain.

resources.title: Post-quantum standards cited in the brief
resources.text: The supplied brief references NIST FIPS 203, 204 and 205 as post-quantum standards relevant to quantum-readiness assessment.

title: GrammaForge: Grammar guided synthetic data Engine for proprietary Languages
fullTitle: GrammaForge: Grammar guided synthetic data Engine for proprietary Languages
problem: Proprietary-language Domain-Specific Language Models face a shortage of training code: public repositories are scarce, while production code can be restricted by privacy, confidentiality or sensitive business logic. Formal grammars exist, but ordinary rule-based generators can produce repetitive, semantically hollow code, and general-purpose LLMs can hallucinate low-resource syntax. Build an intelligent synthetic-data pipeline that uses a formal language grammar, a semantic specification and 5–20 seed programs to produce realistic instruction–response pairs for fine-tuning a proprietary-language DSLM.
audience: Teams developing proprietary-language DSLMs for developers, maintainers and modernization teams that need code completion, explanation, migration or test-generation assistance.
outcome: Produce a diverse, validator-checked fine-tuning dataset with complete grammar coverage, meaningful code and instructions that accurately describe their paired responses, without exposing proprietary production source.

required.title: Grammar, semantics and seeds as inputs
required.text: Accept a formal syntax definition such as BNF, EBNF or an ANTLR grammar, a semantic specification and a small seed set of 5–20 programs.

required.title: Instruction–response training pairs
required.text: Generate a dataset of instruction–response pairs suitable for fine-tuning a proprietary-language DSLM. Each instruction must accurately describe its corresponding response.

required.title: Complete grammar-scope coverage
required.text: Cover the complete grammar scope with a sufficient number of distinct examples for every construct. Include each production rule, alternative and semantic feature enough times for the model to learn it.

required.title: Reference-parser verification
required.text: Ensure responses are syntactically guaranteed by verifying them with the provided reference parser.

required.title: Realistic and diverse code
required.text: Responses must be semantically realistic, avoid near-duplicates and resemble the seed programs in structure and idiom instead of being repetitive or semantically hollow.

optional.title: Recommended generation approaches
optional.text: The brief recommends grammar-constrained LLM decoding, LLM-assisted generation, fine-tuning and probabilistic or learned grammars as possible technologies for the solution.

workflow: Provide a grammar, semantic specification and 5–20 seed programs → generate instruction–response pairs → check syntax with the reference parser → assess semantics, coverage and diversity → remove near-duplicates and check alignment with seed idioms → demonstrate the resulting fine-tuning dataset.

deliverables.title: Working generation pipeline
deliverables.text: Provide a working prototype or pipeline that turns the language specification and seed programs into synthetic training data.

deliverables.title: Coverage demonstration
deliverables.text: Demonstrate coverage in the generated data through a sample demo.

deliverables.title: Architecture and presentation
deliverables.text: Present the system architecture and explain the generation approach.

success.title: Generated-data and semantic validity
success.text: Demonstrate the validity of generated code. Teams may use a language such as COBOL to show this.

success.title: Data diversity
success.text: The generated dataset should provide varied examples rather than near-duplicates.

success.title: DSLM readiness
success.text: The instruction–response data should be suitable for proprietary-language model fine-tuning.

success.title: Scalability and adaptability
success.text: Show how the approach can scale and adapt to different proprietary languages or language versions.

constraints.title: Preserve confidentiality
constraints.text: The source problem treats customer production code as unavailable for training because of privacy policies, confidentiality agreements or sensitive business logic. Generate synthetic data from the language specification rather than exposing proprietary source.

scope.title: Language-agnostic reuse
scope.text: A reusable grammar-to-dataset approach should be adaptable to new proprietary languages by changing the grammar and semantic rules, avoiding the cost of hand-writing training programs at scale.

scope.title: Validator-checked data
scope.text: Quality checks should reduce hallucinated syntax. The same generation approach can also be useful as test-data or fuzzing input for compilers and migration tools; this is supporting context rather than an additional mandatory deliverable.

title: BenchForge: Building a Contamination-Resistant Benchmark for Proprietary-Language Code Models
fullTitle: BenchForge: Building a Contamination-Resistant Benchmark for Proprietary-Language Code Models
problem: Proprietary-language DSLM teams lack public evaluation corpora comparable to HumanEval or MBPP for popular languages. Internal production code cannot simply become a benchmark because of privacy and confidentiality, while small handwritten task sets are costly, cover little of the language and can be overfitted or leaked into training. Use a formal language definition, its semantic rules and a small set of seed examples to build a high-quality, contamination-resistant evaluation benchmark that can compare models, measure fine-tuning gains and reveal regressions.
audience: Teams evaluating proprietary-language code models and deciding whether changes improve model quality or readiness for use.
outcome: Produce a reproducible instruction-to-code benchmark with complete language coverage, verified reference solutions, automatic scoring and meaningful scores for individual constructs.

required.title: Generate from the language specification
required.text: Use the language's formal definition, such as a BNF or ANTLR grammar plus semantic rules, together with a small seed set of examples to build the evaluation benchmark.

required.title: Automatically checkable instruction-to-code tasks
required.text: Each task must contain a natural-language instruction and an automatic way to check a model's response, using executable tests or validator-based property checks.

required.title: Complete grammar coverage
required.text: Cover the complete grammar scope with enough tasks for every construct to produce a statistically meaningful score per construct.

required.title: A range of difficulty
required.text: Include tasks ranging from individual constructs to multi-construct, deeply nested programs.

required.title: Correct references and clear instructions
required.text: Provide verified, correct reference solutions and unambiguous instructions.

required.title: Cheap to rerun and extend
required.text: Make the benchmark inexpensive to rerun and extend so new versions can be generated when the language changes.

optional.title: Recommended benchmark tooling
optional.text: The brief recommends grammar tooling, automatic verification, LLM-assisted instruction writing, LLM-as-judge with human spot checks and instruction-ambiguity detection. These can support task creation and review; each task still requires an automatic checking method.

workflow: Provide grammar, semantic rules and seed examples → generate tasks across constructs and difficulty levels → verify reference solutions and instruction clarity → produce automatic tests or property checks → run the scoring harness on model outputs → report coverage and per-construct results → regenerate or extend the benchmark as the language changes.

deliverables.title: Benchmark generator source code
deliverables.text: Submit the source code for the benchmark generator.

deliverables.title: One-command reproducibility
deliverables.text: Provide a way to reproduce the benchmark with one command.

deliverables.title: Generated benchmark
deliverables.text: Provide the instruction-to-code benchmark with its verified reference solutions and automatic checking methods.

deliverables.title: Evaluation harness
deliverables.text: Include a script that accepts a model's outputs and scores them automatically.

deliverables.title: Coverage report
deliverables.text: Report the benchmark's coverage of the language.

success.title: Grammar and semantic coverage
success.text: Coverage of language constructs and semantic rules.

success.title: Task correctness and clarity
success.text: Correct reference solutions, reliable checks and clear instructions.

success.title: Discriminative power
success.text: The benchmark's ability to distinguish differences in model capability.

success.title: Reproducibility, engineering and report
success.text: Reproducibility of the benchmark, implementation quality and the quality of its report.

success.title: Adaptability to held-out variation
success.text: How well the benchmark approach adapts to held-out variation.

constraints.title: Do not repurpose restricted production code
constraints.text: Internal production code is constrained by privacy policies, client confidentiality and sensitive business logic. Build the benchmark from the formal language definition and seed examples rather than assuming restricted production code can be exposed.

scope.title: Evaluation data, not just a small task list
scope.text: The benchmark must cover the full grammar, support statistically meaningful scores per construct and remain useful for comparing base models, fine-tuning gains and regressions.

scope.title: Contamination resistance
scope.text: Avoid the weakness of a small handwritten benchmark that is easy to overfit to or leak into training. The source requires a contamination-resistant benchmark but does not prescribe a particular prevention method, seed count or numeric task-count threshold.

problem: Apply Quantum Machine Learning (QML) and quantum optimization to identify subtle, non-linear transaction anomalies in high-dimensional, heavily imbalanced financial datasets. The brief describes financial-fraud datasets as typically having millions of rows and fewer than 0.2% fraudulent cases; practical approaches therefore use hybrid quantum-classical architectures.
audience: People building credit-card fraud detection and transaction-anomaly detection systems.
outcome: Demonstrate a hybrid quantum-classical fraud-detection approach, with comparative performance evidence and visible circuit diagnostics.

required.title: Hybrid quantum-classical architecture
required.text: Use classical layers to reduce feature dimensions and quantum circuits to map data into high-dimensional Hilbert spaces for separating complex fraud boundaries.

required.title: Choose a quantum method
required.text: Use QSVM, HQNN, QAE or QAOA methods to solve the problem. These are alternatives in the brief, not a requirement to implement all four.

required.title: Address difficult transaction data
required.text: Work on subtle, non-linear anomalies in high-dimensional, heavily imbalanced financial data.

workflow: Prepare transaction features → reduce dimensions using classical layers → apply the selected quantum method → identify fraud anomalies → compare performance and inspect circuit diagnostics.

problem: Develop an AI-powered system that creates a self-paced training plan for novice engineers from learning materials spread across PDFs, Word documents, presentations, OneNote pages, videos, transcripts and sample programs. The underlying system is complex, its training material has accumulated over decades without proper structure, and much of it is duplicated. Engineers receive different amounts of learning time depending on their team’s workload and need to become productive quickly.
audience: Novice engineers learning a complex system from large, unstructured and duplicated collections of training material.
outcome: Build foundational and production-critical knowledge first, reinforce important concepts, and fit the remaining material into an adaptable on-the-job learning plan.

required.title: Analyze the distributed materials
required.text: Analyze learning material across PDFs, Word documents, presentations, OneNote pages, videos, transcripts and sample programs.

required.title: Structure the knowledge
required.text: Organize the large, unstructured collection and account for duplicated information.

required.title: Identify concepts and relationships
required.text: Identify concepts, prerequisites, dependencies and practical exercises.

required.title: Estimate the complete learning duration
required.text: Automatically estimate the duration needed for a comprehensive learning path.

required.title: Accept the engineer’s time constraints
required.text: Let engineers specify their available learning time. The source example is initial training within 3 weeks followed by 3 hours per week of on-the-job learning; these numbers illustrate configurable constraints, not a fixed schedule for every user.

required.title: Prioritize and defer intelligently
required.text: Prioritize foundational and production-critical knowledge. Defer less essential topics to on-the-job learning while maximizing learning within the available time.

required.title: Assess and reinforce learning
required.text: Schedule assessments and spaced repetition to reinforce important concepts.

workflow: Analyze and structure the learning materials → identify concepts, prerequisites, dependencies and exercises → estimate the full learning duration → accept time constraints → prioritize initial training → schedule assessments, spaced repetition and remaining on-the-job learning.

scope.title: Problem domain
scope.text: AI applied to adaptive, self-paced training for novice engineers.

problem: Design an intelligent Smart Campus Operations System that analyzes campus occupancy, timetable schedules, equipment utilization, weather conditions and simulated or actual electricity consumption. Identify energy wastage and recommend actions that reduce consumption without negatively affecting students or faculty. The emphasis is on predicting, recommending and optimizing campus operations, rather than monitoring energy alone. An illustrative recommendation in the brief describes a computer lab staying powered for 2.5 hours after scheduled use, with a shutdown adjustment estimated to reduce weekly energy consumption by 12%; those figures are an example, not mandatory targets.
audience: Campus operations teams, with student and faculty experience protected while energy use is improved.
outcome: Combine forecasting, optimization and a dashboard to turn campus information into practical, explainable energy-saving recommendations.

required.title: Analyze campus operational inputs
required.text: Analyze occupancy, timetable schedules, equipment utilization, weather conditions and simulated or actual electricity consumption.

required.title: Identify and predict energy wastage

required.title: Recommend and optimize actions
required.text: Recommend actions to reduce consumption without negatively affecting the student or faculty experience.

workflow: Combine campus operational and electricity data → forecast usage and identify wastage → recommend and optimize actions → present the results in a dashboard.

problem: Build an AI system that continuously and privately screens new mothers for early signs of postpartum depression (PPD). The brief describes limited screening visits, stigma, scarce doctors and counselors in rural and low-resource areas, and symptoms emerging between visits in sleep, mood, voice and behavior. Combine questionnaire answers with text or voice check-ins and optional wearable signals. Flag at-risk mothers to a clinician or counselor in time, and never replace clinical diagnosis.
audience: New mothers and the clinicians or counselors who review risk, including people in rural and low-resource settings.
outcome: A private multimodal screening prototype that explains risk trends, supports clinical triage and provides a safe escalation route.

required.title: Continuous, private multimodal screening
required.text: Combine questionnaire answers with text or voice check-ins to screen for early signs of PPD. Wearable signals are optional.

required.title: Clinician or counselor escalation
required.text: Flag at-risk mothers to a clinician or counselor in time. Screening must never replace clinical diagnosis.

required.title: Mother-facing experience
required.text: Provide the screening chatbot and a mother-facing dashboard through a mobile or web app.

required.title: Risk scoring and clinical review
required.text: Provide a trained risk-scoring model and a clinician alert/triage view showing risk level, trend and an explanation of why the mother was flagged.

required.title: Privacy, fairness and safety
required.text: Include consent, careful data handling, a bias and safety review, and an escalation design that covers self-harm indicators.

optional.title: Wearable sensing
optional.text: Optional wearable signals include sleep, heart-rate variability and activity, with edge ML.

workflow: Collect consented questionnaire answers and text or voice check-ins → combine screening signals → score and explain risk trends → show the mother-facing and clinician views → flag risk and refer to a counselor or helpline, with an emergency flow for self-harm indicators.

deliverables.title: Working prototype
deliverables.text: A mobile or web app with the screening chatbot and a mother-facing dashboard.

deliverables.title: Risk-scoring model
deliverables.text: A trained model, for example using EPDS plus text or voice features, with documented accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and false-negative analysis.

deliverables.title: Clinician dashboard
deliverables.text: An alert and triage view showing risk level, trend and the explanation of why a mother was flagged.

deliverables.title: Escalation workflow
deliverables.text: Automatic referral to a counselor or helpline, including an emergency flow for self-harm indicators.

deliverables.title: Privacy and ethics plan
deliverables.text: A consent flow, data handling aligned with HIPAA, GDPR and India’s DPDP as named in the brief, and a bias and safety review.

deliverables.title: Architecture and integration document
deliverables.text: The system design, including a FHIR-based integration approach for hospital systems.

deliverables.title: Demo and pitch
deliverables.text: A short video, a deck and a pilot plan.

deliverables.title: Source code and documentation
deliverables.text: A repository, a README and test results.

success.title: Innovation — 20%
success.text: A novel multimodal approach, with originality beyond a simple questionnaire classifier.

success.title: Feasibility — 20%
success.text: A working prototype, realistic data sources and a credible path to a pilot.

success.title: Impact — 20%
success.text: Potential reach, benefit to mothers and health outcomes, and usefulness in low-resource settings.
